facts: Bletchley Park was the base for Britain's codebreakers during the Second World War, including Alan Turing.
Codebreaking work here is credited with significantly shortening the war.
The site is now a museum telling the story of wartime cryptography and the birth of modern computing.
The Concrete Cows sculpture has become an unofficial, much-loved symbol of Milton Keynes since 1978.
Milton Keynes was designated a new town in 1967, with a distinctive grid-based road system.
The town is known for its extensive network of cycling and walking paths, or 'redways'.
Woburn Abbey has been the seat of the Dukes of Bedford for over 400 years.
Woburn Safari Park, in the abbey's grounds, was one of the first drive-through safari parks in Britain, opened in 1970.
Woburn Sands station is the nearest railhead, with the estate reached by road.
St Albans Cathedral has the longest nave of any cathedral in England.
It stands on the site of the martyrdom of Britain's first Christian saint, Alban.
Verulamium, the Roman town beneath modern St Albans, was once the third-largest town in Roman Britain.
Elizabeth I is said to have learned of her accession to the throne while at Hatfield House in 1558.
The current Jacobean house was built in 1611 by Robert Cecil, chief minister to James I.
Hatfield sits in Hertfordshire, on the East Coast Main Line branch through Welwyn.
Knebworth House has hosted major rock concerts since the 1970s, including Led Zeppelin and Oasis.
The house has been home to the Lytton family since 1490.
Its Gothic exterior was remodelled in the 1840s by novelist Edward Bulwer-Lytton.
Letchworth was the world's first garden city, founded in 1903 by Ebenezer Howard.
It pioneered the idea of planned towns combining housing, industry and green space.
Letchworth influenced garden city and new town planning worldwide.
Welwyn Garden City was founded in 1920 as the second garden city, also by Ebenezer Howard.
The town's grand central avenue and Parkway were designed to give a sense of civic dignity.
It later became one of Britain's post-war new towns as well.

landmark: Stevenage, Britain's first post-war new town
facts: Stevenage was designated in 1946 as the first of Britain's post-war new towns.
It pioneered a fully segregated cycle path network, separate from road traffic.
Stevenage's town centre was one of the first purpose-built pedestrian shopping precincts in Europe.
Hitchin Lavender is one of the largest lavender farms open to the public in England.
The town has one of the largest parish churches in Hertfordshire, St Mary's.
Hitchin was historically a centre of the lavender and rose-growing trade for perfumery.
Shepreth Wildlife Park began as a small animal rescue centre before growing into a full zoo.
The village sits on the River Rhee, close to Cambridge.
Shepreth station is on the line between Cambridge and King's Cross.
King's Lynn was a major member of the medieval Hanseatic League trading network.
The town retains one of the best collections of merchant houses of any English port.
King's Lynn's Custom House, built in 1683, remains a landmark on the historic quayside.
Downham Market's distinctive black-and-white buildings are built from local carrstone.
The town's cast-iron clock tower was erected in 1878.
Downham Market sits on the edge of the Norfolk Fens.
Bond Street has been one of London's most exclusive shopping streets since the 18th century.
The station is a major interchange point for the Elizabeth Line in the West End.
Nearby Oxford Street is one of the busiest shopping streets in Europe.
Canary Wharf's One Canada Square was the tallest building in the UK when completed in 1991.
The area was redeveloped from derelict docklands into a major financial district from the 1980s.
Canary Wharf's Elizabeth Line station has one of the largest underground retail spaces in London.
Centre Point, a 1960s tower beside the station, was one of London's first skyscrapers.
The area is a major hub for London's theatre district and Soho nightlife.
Tottenham Court Road is a key Elizabeth Line and Underground interchange.
The Royal Arsenal at Woolwich produced munitions for the British military for over 200 years.
Arsenal Football Club takes its name from its origins as a works team at the Woolwich Arsenal.
The former Arsenal site has been redeveloped into riverside housing and heritage attractions.
ExCeL London is one of the largest exhibition and convention centres in Europe.
It hosted boxing, weightlifting and other events during the 2012 Olympics.
Custom House station sits directly beside the venue on the Elizabeth Line.
Heathrow is the busiest airport in Europe by passenger numbers.
The Elizabeth Line provides a direct rail link from central London to the airport terminals.
Heathrow opened as a small airfield in 1929 before its major post-war expansion.
The Natural History Museum at Tring holds the vast personal collection of Walter Rothschild, including thousands of taxidermy specimens.
Tring sits in the Chiltern Hills, on the Grand Union Canal.
Tring station is over a mile from the town centre, in the Bulbourne valley.
William the Conqueror received the submission of Saxon nobles at Berkhamsted Castle in 1066.
The castle's earthworks and moat remain well preserved today.
Author Graham Greene grew up in Berkhamsted, where his father was headmaster of the school.
The Hemel Hempstead Water Gardens were designed in the 1950s as part of the town's new town development.
Hemel Hempstead was designated a post-war new town in 1947.
The town sits in the Gade Valley, in the Chiltern Hills.
Watford Junction is a major interchange on the West Coast Main Line, just north of London.
The town's football club, Watford FC, plays at nearby Vicarage Road.
Watford Junction connects London Northwestern services to both London Euston and St Albans.
The Leighton Buzzard Railway is a narrow-gauge heritage line, originally built to serve sand quarries.
The town's name is thought to combine an Anglo-Saxon personal name with a reference to a historic manor.
Leighton Buzzard sits on the Grand Union Canal.
Northampton was the centre of the English shoemaking industry for centuries.
The Northampton Museum holds one of the largest shoe collections in the world.
Northampton is one of the largest towns in England without city status.
Tamworth was once the capital of the Anglo-Saxon kingdom of Mercia.
Tamworth Castle's Norman motte sits above the meeting of the Rivers Tame and Anker.
The town is home to Drayton Manor, a large theme park.
Atherstone hosts a unique annual Shrove Tuesday street football game, played since medieval times.
The town was historically a centre of English hat manufacturing.
Atherstone sits on the historic Roman road Watling Street.
Alexandra Palace hosted the world's first regular high-definition TV broadcasts, from a BBC studio in 1936.
The building has been substantially rebuilt after two major fires.
It stands on a hill offering sweeping views across London.
Islington has one of the largest concentrations of Georgian terraces and squares in London.
Arsenal's former Highbury stadium stood a short walk from the station until 2006.
Highbury & Islington is a major interchange for several rail and Underground lines.
Moorgate sits at the northern edge of the City of London's financial district.
The station takes its name from a former gate in the medieval City wall.
Moorgate was the site of a serious rail crash in 1975, prompting new safety systems on the Underground.
Finsbury Park was one of the first purpose-built public parks in Victorian London, opened in 1869.
The park hosts major outdoor concerts and events throughout the year.
Finsbury Park is a major interchange between several rail and Underground lines.
The roundabout above Old Street station became known as 'Silicon Roundabout' for its concentration of tech start-ups.
Old Street sits on the boundary of Hackney and Islington.
The area has transformed from light industry into a major tech hub since the 2000s.
Romford has held a market charter since 1247, still trading today.
The town was historically the centre of the Liberty of Havering, a self-governing royal manor.
Romford is a major interchange station in east London.
Ilford developed rapidly as a London suburb following the arrival of the railway in the 1830s.
The town was historically part of the ancient Hundred of Becontree.
Ilford sits in the London Borough of Redbridge.
Brentwood sits at the edge of Greater London, on the boundary with rural Essex.
The town's name derives from a burnt clearing in the surrounding forest.
Brentwood has become associated with reality television following a popular ITV series set there.
Potters Bar sits just inside the M25, on the edge of Hertfordshire's green belt.
The town developed largely as a commuter suburb following railway electrification.
Potters Bar station is on the East Coast Main Line.
Cuffley sits within the Hertfordshire green belt, close to Northaw Great Wood.
The village was the site of the first Zeppelin to be shot down over Britain, in 1916.
Cuffley is the terminus of a short branch line from Enfield.
Hertford is the county town of Hertfordshire, with origins dating to Anglo-Saxon times.
The town's castle, though much altered, has royal connections dating back centuries.
Hertford North serves the Hertford Loop line via Stevenage.
Royston Cave is a mysterious man-made chamber carved with medieval religious carvings, rediscovered in 1742.
The town sits at the crossing of two ancient routes, Ermine Street and the Icknield Way.
Royston straddles the Hertfordshire and Cambridgeshire border.
Biggleswade was historically an important centre for market gardening in Bedfordshire.
The town sits on the Great North Road, an ancient route between London and Scotland.
Biggleswade is on the East Coast Main Line between Hitchin and Sandy.
The RSPB, Britain's largest nature conservation charity, has its headquarters at The Lodge near Sandy.
The reserve includes heathland and woodland managed for wildlife.
Sandy sits on the Great Ouse river system in Bedfordshire.
Oliver Cromwell was born in Huntingdon in 1599 and later became the town's MP.
The Cromwell Museum occupies the school building where he was educated.
Huntingdon sits on the Great Ouse in Cambridgeshire.
St Neots is the largest town in Cambridgeshire, on the banks of the Great Ouse.
The town takes its name from the relics of St Neot, brought to a priory here in the 10th century.
St Neots hosts regular riverside festivals and events.
Waterbeach sits on the edge of the Cambridgeshire Fens, close to the River Cam.
The village has grown rapidly as part of Cambridge's wider commuter area.
Waterbeach is a stop on the line between Cambridge and Ely.
Littleport was the site of a significant 1816 riot over rural poverty and wages.
The village sits in the heart of the Cambridgeshire Fens, reclaimed farmland below sea level.
Littleport is on the line between Ely and King's Lynn.
Watlington sits in the flat Norfolk Fens, close to King's Lynn.
The village developed around agriculture in the reclaimed fenland.
Watlington station is on the line towards King's Lynn.
Drayton Park station sits close to Arsenal's Emirates Stadium, opened in 2006.
The area is within the London Borough of Islington.
Drayton Park is on the branch line towards Moorgate.
Chadwell Heath developed rapidly as a London suburb in the early 20th century.
The area sits within the London Borough of Barking and Dagenham.
Chadwell Heath is on the Great Eastern Main Line towards Essex.
Forest Gate developed rapidly with Victorian terraced housing from the 1870s.
The area takes its name from a former gate into Epping Forest.
Forest Gate sits in the London Borough of Newham.
Frogmore Paper Mill was the site of the world's first successful continuous paper-making machine, in 1803.
The mill sits on the River Gade in Hertfordshire.
Apsley developed around the paper-making industry that grew up along the Grand Union Canal.
